functions.sig: void SetElemRect(EHudElem E, float X, float Y, float W, float H);
functions.doc: Record where an element drew this frame (for the edit handles). Harmless outside edit mode - it's a couple of float stores.

functions.name: DrawEditOverlay
functions.doc: Draggable handles + toolbar over every element while Edit UI is open.

functions.name: DrawSpellbook
functions.doc: The Combat Abilities & Spells panel.

functions.name: DrawSpellButton
functions.doc: On-screen button (next to the cog) that opens the spellbook.

functions.name: DrawSpellBars
functions.doc: The 4 persistent spell bars (10 slots each), separate from the Action Bar. Drawn every frame on foot, like the Action Bar - clickable when the cursor is free, and bar 1 always responds to the keyboard number row.

classes.name: UCosmicInventoryComponent
classes.doc: Bag + equipment in one lean component (fab-market friendly: one class to add, no blueprint dependencies). The bag is a fixed grid of item slots; equipment is one item per ECosmicEquipSlot. Equip/unequip move items between the two.

functions.name: AddItem
functions.doc: Add to the first empty bag slot. False if the bag is full.

functions.name: EquipFromBag
functions.doc: Equip the item in a bag slot into its own Slot (swaps with any current).

functions.name: UnequipToBag
functions.doc: Unequip a slot back into the bag. False if the bag is full.

functions.name: GetBag
functions.sig: const TArray<FCosmicItemDef>& GetBag() const { return Bag; }

functions.name: GetMainHand
functions.doc: Convenience: currently held weapon defs (invalid def if empty-handed).

properties.name: BagSize
properties.doc: Bag capacity (fixed grid).

properties.name: Bag
properties.doc: Bag: fixed size, invalid defs = empty slots.

properties.name: Equipped
properties.doc: Equipment keyed by slot.

classes.name: FCosmicItemDef
classes.doc: Item data model for the Cosmos plugin. Pure C++ (no blueprint assets needed): an item is a struct value, an inventory is an array of them. The ItemType is what drives combat behavior and (later) which animation plays when triggered (1hs / 2hs / 1hb / 2hb / piercing / laser / torpedo).

functions.name: IsValid
functions.sig: bool IsValid() const { return ItemId != NAME_None; }

properties.name: Slot
properties.doc: Slot this item equips into (None = not equippable, bag-only).

properties.name: Power
properties.doc: Base damage (melee swing or in-flight shot) / armor value for Armor.

classes.name: ACosmicItemPickup
classes.doc: A world item: floats, spins, and auto-adds to the inventory of any character that walks into it. Spawn one with SpawnPickup() or drop from kills later.

functions.name: SpawnPickup
functions.sig: static ACosmicItemPickup* SpawnPickup(UWorld* World, const FVector& Location, const FCosmicItemDef& Def);
functions.doc: Spawn helper (sets the def + tint in one call).

classes.name: FCosmicMeleeMoveset
classes.doc: Swing clips for one body, keyed by the WEAPON TYPE being swung. File scope, not nested in the component: UnrealHeaderTool does not allow a USTRUCT inside a UCLASS.

classes.name: UCosmicMeleeComponent
classes.doc: On-foot combat driven by held items. LMB swings the main hand, RMB the off hand (unarmed strikes when a hand is empty). The item's TYPE (1hs/2hs/1hb/ 2hb/piercing) selects a swing profile - reach, speed, damage, arc - which is also the hook animation blueprints will key off later. Flight weapons (laser/torpedo) are handled by UCosmicWeaponsComponent and only fire in flight; this component only acts on foot.

functions.name: SetAnimationCharacter
functions.doc: Which body is currently worn, and therefore which montage to swing with. Set by UCosmicAppearanceComponent through SetAnimationCharacter, the same call and the same moment the ability component gets it. Both have to move together: an appearance swap that updated one and not the other would give a character casting with the right clip and swinging with a clip bound to the body it used to be wearing.

functions.name: ResolveSwingMontage
functions.doc: Resolves the clip for the worn body and the weapon being swung. Null when none is configured.

functions.name: GetMainCooldown
functions.doc: HUD read-back: seconds remaining on each hand's swing (0 = ready).

functions.name: GetLastSwingType
functions.doc: The type of the last swing (drives which animation to play when wired).

properties.name: SwingMovesets
properties.doc: tables rather than one with a character argument threaded through it. Movesets by worn body ("Aurora", "Zinx"), keyed the same way the appearance catalog and UCosmicAbilityComponent::SetAnimationCharacter key theirs, so there is one vocabulary rather than two. A missing character or a missing weapon type is a working state: melee behaves as it did before this existed - damage lands, nothing animates. THE OUTER KEY IS A WORKAROUND FOR THREE SKELETONS. Section 10's shared-skeleton migration deletes it: one skeleton means one clip per weapon serves every body.

classes.name: ACosmicNebulaField
classes.doc: Distant nebulae and galaxies that actually LIGHT the arena. The problem this solves is not decoration, it is illumination. Everything in this arena wears automotive chrome and brushed metal - near-perfect mirrors - and a mirror in empty black space reflects nothing, so it reads as a flat grey cut-out no matter how many directional lights are aimed at it. Two directional lights give you two highlights and nothing else. What metal needs is an ENVIRONMENT to reflect. So this actor builds one: * a SKYLIGHT in SLS_CapturedScene mode, which captures the surrounding emissive geometry and feeds it ba…

functions.name: RebuildField
functions.doc: Tear down and rebuild the whole field from the current properties.

properties.name: SkyLightIntensity
properties.doc: Ambient light captured from the nebulae. This is the single most important number here for making the arena readable - it is what fills the shadow side of every planet instead of leaving it pure black.

properties.name: SkyLightColor
properties.doc: Tint applied to that ambient. A faint blue-violet reads as deep space; pure white reads as a studio.

properties.name: NebulaCount
properties.doc: How many nebula shells to place around the arena.

properties.name: FieldRadius
properties.doc: Distance from this actor to the shells (cm). Should sit at or beyond the arena boundary so they read as background, never as obstacles.

properties.name: NebulaSizeMin
properties.doc: Size range of a single shell (cm). Deliberately enormous: these are galaxies, and at this distance anything small vanishes.

properties.name: NebulaGlow
properties.doc: Emissive brightness of the shells.

properties.name: NebulaOpacity
properties.doc: Opacity of each shell. Low by design - they should suggest gas, and stack into something denser where several overlap.

properties.name: SwirlDegreesPerSecond
properties.doc: Degrees per second of slow swirl. Very low: at this scale anything faster reads as a spinning prop rather than a galaxy.

properties.name: AccentIntensity
properties.doc: Point-light brightness co-located with the brightest shells (candelas), so the ambient has a direction instead of being uniform fill.

properties.name: AccentLightCount
properties.doc: How many of the shells also carry an accent light. Kept small - each one is a real light in the scene.

properties.name: NebulaMesh
properties.doc: Mesh for a shell. A sphere is expected; the engine's basic sphere is loaded automatically if this is left empty.

properties.name: NebulaMaterial
properties.doc: Material for the shells. An emissive/translucent material is expected - M_Atmosphere from the cosmic demo set works well and is used by default.

properties.name: NebulaSystem
properties.doc: OPTIONAL authored Niagara nebula. If set, it is spawned instead of the emissive shells - the shells exist because a Niagara system has to be authored in the editor and cannot be generated from code.

properties.name: Seed
properties.doc: Deterministic layout seed, so the field looks identical every run.

classes.name: ACosmicPlayerCameraManager
classes.doc: Camera manager that makes on-foot mouse look work on a spherical planet. The default APlayerCameraManager applies mouse yaw around WORLD +Z and pitch around the world horizontal. That only feels right when the view has zero roll. To keep the horizon level on a sphere the control rotation must carry a roll, and world-frame yaw/pitch on a rolled rotation tumbles (the "axes spin around" bug). This override instead applies the mouse delta in the player's LOCAL gravity frame - yaw around the planet's up, pitch around the local right - then re-levels the roll and clamps the elevation. Off foot (fly…

functions.name: ProcessViewRotation
functions.sig: virtual void ProcessViewRotation(float DeltaTime, FRotator& OutViewRotation, FRotator& OutDeltaRot) override;

properties.name: WalkPitchLimit
properties.doc: Elevation limit above/below the local horizon while walking (degrees).

properties.name: SnapReportDegrees
properties.doc: Log a line whenever the view jumps more than this in one frame (degrees). The camera snap has survived two fixes made by reading the code, so this exists to stop the third one being another guess. It reports the ACTUAL angle between last frame's forward and this frame's, plus which branch produced it and what the inputs were - which is the one thing static reading cannot tell you. OFF by default now that the cause is known and fixed (see MaxLookDeltaDegrees). Set it to 8 to turn the diagnostic back on if the view ever starts jumping again - it costs one dot product per frame and only formats a string when something actually moves that far.

properties.name: MaxLookDeltaDegrees
properties.doc: - it is nearly pure pitch while yaw stays under a degree, where a hand moving that fast would smear across both axes; - ordinary frames in the same session peak around 20 degrees. The cause is the OS cursor being recentred against the viewport edge under LockOnCapture: one frame reports the whole jump back across the window. It is a windowing artefact, which is why it is worse in PIE, and why it survived every change to the rotation maths. 45 degrees is chosen to sit above real input and below the spike. At 60 fps that is a 2700 deg/sec flick - faster than anyone aims, slower than a warp. A dropped frame costs one frame of look; an accepted spike costs the shot you were lining up.

classes.name: UCosmicPlayerRepComponent
classes.doc: The Cosmos plugin's per-player replication channel. WHY THIS EXISTS. See PROJECT.md section 13, "Decision needed before P1, P2 and P7 - the carrier problem". Short version: a server RPC has to travel on an object the sending connection owns, and a replicated property has to live on an object that itself replicates. Before this component existed, UCosmicFlightComponent was the only thing in the Cosmos plugin that qualified - it is a DEFAULT SUBOBJECT (so no content block; see ARSSCharacter::CosmicFlight for why that matters), it replicates, and the owning client's connection owns it, so server…

functions.name: Server_ReportState
functions.doc: Owning client -> server. UNRELIABLE on purpose: this is a stream of snapshots at ~30 Hz, and a dropped one is stale by the time it would have been resent. Mode edges are protected by being published the instant they change (see UCosmicFlightComponent::PublishLocalState), not by reliability.

functions.name: PublishState
functions.doc: Owner-side: get a freshly captured state onto the wire. A straight property write on the authority (listen-server host, AI); a Server RPC everywhere else. Callers decide WHETHER to publish (movement authority, rate limiting, NaN guards - see UCosmicFlightComponent::PublishLocalState); this decides HOW.

functions.name: Server_ReportMountVisual
functions.doc: Owner -> server, once. Reliable: this fires a handful of times per session and a dropped one leaves a player flying a cone until they change mounts.

functions.name: PublishMountVisual
functions.doc: Owner-side: publish a mount configuration. See UCosmicFlightComponent::PublishMountVisual, which builds the value from its own MountMeshAsset/Scale/Rotation/Offset and calls this.

functions.name: Server_ReportCombatState
functions.doc: Owner -> server. RELIABLE, unlike the movement stream: these are LATCHES, not samples. Dropping the packet that clears bIsAttacking leaves a remote player swinging forever, and no later packet necessarily comes along to correct it - the next one arrives when they attack again, which might be never.

functions.name: PublishCombatState
functions.doc: Owner-side: get a combat state onto the wire. Same authority/RPC split as PublishState. Callers decide WHEN (on change only - see ARSSCharacter::Tick); this decides how.

functions.name: GetLocalCombat
functions.doc: Poll for the authored state, expiring it when the swing's time is up. NOT const, and there is no timer: this component does not tick (bCanEverTick = false, deliberately - it is a mailbox, not a simulation). ARSSCharacter::Tick already polls every frame on exactly the machine that authors this, so expiry rides along with the read that was happening anyway and no second scheduler is introduced.

functions.name: Server_ReportAppearance
functions.doc: Owner -> server. RELIABLE: like the combat latches, this is a state, not a sample. A dropped packet here leaves a player wearing the wrong body on every other screen with nothing scheduled to correct it.

functions.name: PublishAppearance
functions.doc: Owner-side publish. Does NOT apply locally - the caller has already done that, so the player who pressed the key sees the change on the same frame rather than after a round trip. This puts it on the wire for everyone else.

functions.name: RequestCelestialImpulse
functions.sig: void RequestCelestialImpulse(ACelestialBody* Body, const FVector& LocalPoint, const FVector& DeltaV);
functions.doc: Ask the server to shove a celestial body on this client's behalf. Moved here from UCosmicFlightComponent unchanged in behaviour - see the file header above for why the carrier lives here now instead of on a component named for flight. Callers should go through UCelestialSubsystem::RequestImpulseAtPoint rather than reaching for this directly.

functions.name: Server_RequestCelestialImpulse
functions.sig: void Server_RequestCelestialImpulse(ACelestialBody* Body, FVector AbsolutePoint, FVector DeltaV);

properties.name: NetState
properties.doc: The newest state this pawn's owner published. Written by the owning client through Server_ReportState, or directly by the authority when the authority is the one holding the input (listen-server host, AI). COND_SkipOwner: the owner is the AUTHOR of this value. Sending it back would spend bandwidth telling players where they already know they are, and OnRep would start feeding their own round-tripped position into the proxy interpolator, which must never run on a pawn we simulate.

properties.name: MountVisual
properties.doc: Which ship this player flies. Published once by the owner; read by proxies.

properties.name: CombatState
properties.doc: The owner's current combat state. Read by proxies; see FCosmicCombatState. No OnRep. The owning character polls this each tick and copies it into its own IRSSAnimStateProvider fields, which is both simpler than an event and more robust: a proxy that joins late, or one whose character swapped mesh mid-combo, picks the value up on its very next tick rather than having to have been listening at the moment it changed.

properties.name: LocalCombat
properties.doc: Authored on the input-holding machine only. Never on the wire - what goes on the wire is `CombatState`, published by ARSSCharacter::Tick on change.

properties.name: Appearance
properties.doc: NOT COND_SkipOwner, unlike NetState and MountVisual. Those are streams the owner is authoritative over and must never be echoed back. This is a latch, so it goes to everyone including the owner: it is what makes a LATE JOINER see the bodies people are already wearing, which is the case the whole thing exists for. OnRep_Appearance is a no-op when the look is already correct, which is the owner's usual case. TRANSIENT, AND THEREFORE NOT PERSISTENT. This lives on the pawn's component and dies with the pawn, so an appearance does NOT currently survive a respawn or a server change - nothing re-publishes it, and the hub does not store it. Making it stick means writing it into the character record through UPhxServerAuth::SaveCharacter and applying it on spawn; that is a separate piece of work, not an accident of this one.

classes.name: ACosmicPocketDoor
classes.doc: Cosmos - sliding pocket door. A slab that retracts sideways into the wall it sits in, the way a pocket door does. It is not a portal and it does not teleport anyone: what is on the other side is on the other side, in the same world, and you walk through. Built for the Holo-sim entrance on the station deck, but nothing here knows about Holo-sims. It is a door.

functions.name: SetLocked
functions.sig: void SetLocked(bool bNewLocked, const FText& Reason);
functions.doc: Server-only. Locking a door that is open closes it first.

functions.name: OnConstruction
functions.sig: virtual void OnConstruction(const FTransform& Transform) override;
functions.doc: AActor

properties.name: DoorWidth
properties.doc: Opening width, cm. The slab is this wide and retracts by this much.

properties.name: RetractDirection
properties.doc: Which way the slab retracts, in local space. +Y slides right. A pocket door needs somewhere to go. The wall it disappears into is the caller's problem - this only guarantees the slab ends up DoorWidth away along this axis, so a wall of at least that width on this side hides it.

properties.name: TravelSeconds
properties.doc: Seconds for a full open or close.

properties.name: bAutoOpenOnApproach
properties.doc: Open when a pawn steps into the trigger volume.

properties.name: ApproachRange
properties.doc: How far out the trigger reaches from the opening, cm.

properties.name: AutoCloseDelay
properties.doc: Seconds with nobody in range before it closes. 0 keeps it open.

properties.name: bLocked
properties.doc: A locked door will not open, for any reason, including approach. Server-authoritative and replicated, because whether a Holo-sim will let you in is a decision the hub makes and the client only displays. A client that flipped this locally would open a door onto a room it still could not be admitted to, which is a confusing way to be refused.

properties.name: LockedMessage
properties.doc: Shown by the UI when a locked door is approached.

properties.name: TrimMaterial
properties.doc: Emissive. Used for the frame strip, which is how the state reads at a glance.

properties.name: OpenAlpha
properties.doc: 0 closed, 1 fully retracted. Replicated so a late joiner sees a door that is already open as open, rather than watching it play the animation.

classes.name: ACosmicSkyDirector
classes.doc: Cosmos - re-anchors a single flat-world sky onto whichever body you are on. THE PROBLEM THIS IS SOLVING, STATED HONESTLY. UltraDynamicSky (and every sky system like it) assumes ONE world: a sky sphere centred near the camera, a horizon at world Z, clouds on a world-Z plane, fog measured from world Z, and a sun placed by time-of-day in that same frame. This game has ~100 spherical bodies with radial gravity and no global up. One sky actor cannot serve them, and nothing about the sky asset expects to be rotated. So this does not try to make UDS understand spheres. It moves the whole sky rig so…

functions.name: GetSkyOpacity
functions.doc: Current opacity, 0 in space and 1 at the surface.

functions.name: OnSkyAnchored
functions.sig: void OnSkyAnchored(ACelestialBody* Body, float Opacity, const FVector& SunDirection);
functions.doc: Fires every frame the sky is anchored, after the transform is applied. Do the UDS-specific work here: set its opacity/intensity from Opacity, and drive time of day from SunDirection if you want the star to be the sun rather than UDS's own clock. SunDirection is world-space, from the player toward the system's star.

functions.name: OnSkyHidden
functions.doc: Fires once when the sky goes fully invisible, so Blueprint can hide the rig.

functions.name: MakeSkyMovable
functions.doc: Promote the sky rig's components to Movable. Not a convenience. A Static component REFUSES to move and only says so in a per-frame warning, so a sky left Static makes this entire class a no-op that looks like it is working. UDS ships Static because its home world has a sky that never travels.

functions.name: DriveSkyTime
functions.sig: void DriveSkyTime(const FVector& SunDirection, const FVector& Up, const FVector& North);
functions.doc: Push the sun's local elevation into the sky as an hour of the day. REFLECTION, deliberately. Ultra Dynamic Sky is a Blueprint asset with no C++ type to link against, and making Cosmos depend on a marketplace plugin to compile would be a bad trade for one float. Setting the property by name costs a lookup, works with any sky that exposes an hours value, and degrades to a single warning when it does not.

properties.name: SkyActor
properties.doc: The sky rig to move. Point this at your Ultra_Dynamic_Sky actor. A plain AActor reference on purpose: UDS is a Blueprint asset with no C++ type to link against, and Cosmos must not gain a dependency on a marketplace plugin. Anything with a sky sphere and a directional light works here.

properties.name: bAnchorToStableGround
properties.doc: Also re-anchor to the station, not just to celestial bodies. The deck has a definite up and an enclosed volume, so a sky over it is coherent - but it is a hangar in space, and a cloud layer inside it is absurd. Off by default; turn it on only if you build an open-air deck.

properties.name: AtmosphereFraction
properties.doc: Altitude at which the sky has fully faded out, as a fraction of the body's radius above its surface. The sky is only correct near the player, so it has to be gone before the player can see it from outside. 0.35 of a radius is high enough to fly around in and low enough that you never see a cloud layer edge-on from space.

properties.name: ReanchorDegreesPerSecond
properties.doc: How fast the rig rotates to a new body, degrees per second. Not instant. Stepping off one planet onto another can flip the local up by 180 degrees, and snapping the horizon through that reads as the world inverting. Easing it makes the transition legible - and the fade means most of the swing happens while the sky is invisible anyway.

properties.name: bHideWhenFaded
properties.doc: Hide the sky rig outright once it has faded out. The blunt version of an opacity fade, and it needs no cooperation from the sky asset. A sky sphere seen from outside is worse than no sky, so when the player is high enough that it would be visible edge-on, it is simply gone.

properties.name: bRequireAtmosphere
properties.doc: Only show the sky on bodies that actually have an atmosphere. This is the setting that keeps a terrestrial sky system from making a space game look like a flight sim. UDS renders blue scattering, cloud decks and ground fog; on an airless rock all three are wrong, and running it everywhere is what made the visuals read as "wild". Reads ACelestialBody::bHasAtmosphere, which the world builder rolls per planet and which also drives the visible shell - so the sky underfoot and the halo seen from orbit are the same fact. Turn it off only to preview the sky on every body.

properties.name: bFadeWithVisibleShell
properties.doc: Take the fade ceiling from the body's own visible atmosphere shell. The companion to bRequireAtmosphere: that one decides WHICH bodies have a sky, this one makes the sky end where the atmosphere you can see ends. ShellScale is the halo's radius as a multiple of the body's, so ShellScale - 1 is its thickness in radii (0.12 for the builder's atmospheres) and AtmosphereFraction below becomes the fallback for bodies with no shell. Off means the two are independent again, which is how the sky came to extend three times higher than the haze it was supposed to be part of.

properties.name: bDriveTimeOfDay
properties.doc: Drive the sky's time of day from the REAL star instead of its own clock. Set by reflection, by name, so Cosmos never links against the sky plugin. If the property is missing or renamed this quietly does nothing and says so once - which is the right failure for an optional integration.

properties.name: TimeOfDayPropertyName
properties.doc: Name of the sky's time-of-day property, in hours (0-24). "Time of Day" is Ultra Dynamic Sky's. Blueprint property names keep their spaces, which is why this is a display-name string rather than an identifier.

properties.name: RefreshFunctionName
properties.doc: Function to call after changing the time, so the sky rebuilds itself. UDS does not react to the property alone; it recalculates on this call. Left empty, the value is set and nothing refreshes until the sky's own tick gets to it.

classes.name: UCosmicSkySettings
classes.doc: Project-wide sky configuration. Project Settings -> Game -> Cosmos Sky. The sky class is deliberately a SOFT reference and deliberately empty by default. Soft, so a world that will never build a sky never loads half a gigabyte to find that out; empty, so nothing silently half-works if the marketplace plugin is absent or its blueprint moves.

functions.name: GetCategoryName
functions.sig: virtual FName GetCategoryName() const override { return TEXT("Game"); }

properties.name: SkyActorClass
properties.doc: The sky rig to spawn. Point this at Ultra_Dynamic_Sky. Left empty the subsystem builds nothing and says so once, which is the right failure for an optional integration - better than a half-built sky nobody asked for.

properties.name: DirectorClass
properties.doc: Director class that re-anchors the rig to the body underfoot. Defaults to ACosmicSkyDirector. Override only to use a Blueprint child that also drives weather or cloud coverage.

properties.name: bOnlyInHoloSims
properties.doc: Build a sky only in holo-sim instances. The whole point. Turning this off puts the sky back in the persistent world, which is what it looked like before - useful for previewing the asset, wrong for shipping.

properties.name: DefaultHoloSimSky
properties.doc: Sky used by a holo-sim that has not specified one. None, because a holo-sim starts as an empty grid room in space. A sim whose spec asks for a planet calls ApplySkyMode and gets one.

classes.name: UCosmicSkySubsystem
classes.doc: Builds and tears down the sky rig for the world it belongs to. Nothing is spawned until something asks for it, so the persistent world pays nothing - not the memory, not the extra directional light, not the fog.

functions.name: ApplySkyMode
functions.doc: Set the sky for this world, spawning or destroying the rig as needed. Safe to call repeatedly and safe to call late - which matters, because a holo-sim's spec arrives from the hub asynchronously, well after the world has started. Calling it with the mode already in effect does nothing.

functions.name: IsHoloSimProcess
functions.doc: True if this process was launched as a holo-sim instance. Reads -HoloSimId= directly rather than asking the game mode, so Cosmos stays independent of PhxAccount. See the file header.

classes.name: FCosmicStationKit
classes.doc: close, and the reference image was only ever about SHAPE. These are authored meshes with bevels, recessed fields, ribs and bolt heads, so the same silhouette survives being walked up to. Soft paths rather than hard references, matching the rest of the schema: a Holo-sim spec arriving as JSON from the hub can name an asset but cannot carry one. Anything left empty is skipped rather than substituted - a missing pylon is a hole you notice, whereas a stand-in cube is the thing this replaced. Built by Scripts/import_station_kit.py from the .fbx files in Art/StationKit. (No wildcard in that path on…

properties.name: PlateSize
properties.doc: UNUSED BY THE HULL. Kept for the deck, which is still tiled. Plate count goes as 1/PlateSize^2, so this is the main performance dial. At the authored 2,400 a 1.2 km hull needs ~7,800 plates and the frame rate dips whenever you fly close enough for them all to resolve. Instancing them at 2x (4,800 cm = 48 m) quarters that to ~2,000 with no visible loss - a plate is still under a twelfth of the hull's radius. Instances are SCALED to this from the authored 24 m mesh, so changing it does not require a re-export.

properties.name: AuthoredPlateSize
properties.doc: Authored edge length of the plate MESH, cm. Only change this on re-export.

properties.name: AuthoredShellRadius
properties.doc: Radius the hull shells import at, in UNREAL UNITS. 100, not 1. The shells are authored at radius 1 in Blender METRES, and Blender's FBX exporter applies a 100x unit scale on the way out because Unreal works in centimetres. So a "unit" sphere arrives 100 uu across. Getting this wrong is not subtle: treating them as radius 1 and scaling by HullRadius built a 60 km station instead of a 600 m one, which swallowed the entire solar system. Every shell placement divides by this.

properties.name: HullUpper
properties.doc: The hull shells. UNIT RADIUS - scaled to HullRadius at build time. ONE MESH EACH, not a field of plates. Tiling a sphere with squares is geometrically impossible without gaps: a square grid on a sphere has to stretch or tear, and it tore - visible holes all over the dome. It also cost ~2,000 instances, which is where the frame rate near the shell went. The panel detail is modelled INTO the shell as inset faces, so it still reads as plating up close, with real seams and no possible gap.

classes.name: ACosmicStation
classes.doc: Cosmos - procedural orbital station. A Privateer-style hub: a blocky sphere with an equatorial band cut clean through it, a shaft down through the north pole, and a landing deck filling the whole middle. Aircraft enter from any side, or straight down through the top, into one shared hangar volume. EVERYTHING IS INSTANCED. The hull is not a mesh - it is several thousand box instances laid over a sphere, jittered in size and depth, with lit windows and greeble clusters scattered across them. That is not a compromise for the sake of the pipeline; it is what the reference actually looks like. It…

functions.name: GetDeckCenterWorld
functions.doc: World-space centre of the landing deck's top face. Where a PlayerStart goes.

functions.name: GetDeckRadius
functions.doc: Radius of the deck's top face, cm. Derived from the hull, never set by hand.

functions.name: GetDeckSurfaceZ
functions.doc: Height of the deck's top face in station-local space.

functions.name: GetHoloSimDoorWorld
functions.sig: bool GetHoloSimDoorWorld(FVector& OutLocation, FRotator& OutRotation) const;
functions.doc: World transform for the Holo-sim door: standing on the deck, set into the entrance building's face, opening out across the hangar. False when the entrance was not built, which is the only honest answer - returning the deck centre instead would put a door in the middle of the landing area.

functions.name: GetKeepOutRadius
functions.doc: Clearance the world builder should keep around the station, cm. Not a free parameter - it is whatever the geometry works out to, docking arms included. Deriving it means the planet field's keep-out cannot disagree with the station that is actually there.

functions.name: IsDeckSpaceReserved
functions.sig: bool IsDeckSpaceReserved(double X, double Y, double Margin) const;
functions.doc: True if this deck-local XY belongs to the holo-sim entrance or its approach. Exists because the clutter pass and the entrance pass were placing into the same space with no knowledge of each other, and the clutter won: stacked containers and gantries landed on the doorway and across the sightline to it. Anything that scatters objects on the deck must ask this first. Margin is added on all sides - pass roughly the placed object's own footprint, since only its centre is being tested.

functions.name: Rebuild
functions.doc: Tear down and rebuild every instance. Safe to call repeatedly.

functions.name: OnConstruction
functions.sig: virtual void OnConstruction(const FTransform& Transform) override;
functions.doc: AActor

functions.name: AddPiece
functions.sig: void AddPiece(ECosmicStationBucket Bucket, const FTransform& Xf);
functions.doc: Add one box. Centre and half-extent are in cm; the engine cube is 100 cm, so the scale is HalfExtent/50. Every caller works in real dimensions and none of them has to remember that.

functions.name: MeshFor
functions.doc: The mesh a bucket draws, or null when the kit does not name one.

functions.name: BucketCollides
functions.doc: Does this bucket collide? Decorative pieces do not - see the enum.

functions.name: IsCutAway
functions.sig: bool IsCutAway(const FVector& UnitDir, double Radius) const;
functions.doc: True if this direction falls in the band or the polar shaft, i.e. is cut away.

properties.name: HullRadius
properties.doc: Hull radius, cm. 60,000 gives a 1.2 km sphere.

properties.name: SlotHalfHeight
properties.doc: Half-height of the equatorial band, cm. The band is a gap between two hemispheres, open all the way around except where the pylons cross it. 15,000 gives a 300 m mouth - wide enough to fly into at cruise without an autopilot, tight enough that the station still reads as solid rather than as two plates on sticks.

properties.name: PolarShaftRadius
properties.doc: Radius of the shaft bored down through the north pole, cm. 0 closes it.

properties.name: PylonCount
properties.doc: Structural columns spanning the band. They are what stops the silhouette reading as a cage: with none, the two hemispheres float apart; with too many, the openings close up. Eight gives eight ~45-degree mouths, which is what "enter from any side" needs to be true rather than nearly true.

properties.name: DockingArmCount
properties.doc: Arms radiating from the equator, each ending in a docking pod.

properties.name: bSecondaryModule
properties.doc: A smaller sphere slung below the hull on a neck, as in the reference.

properties.name: SecondaryModuleScale
properties.doc: Secondary module radius as a fraction of HullRadius.

properties.name: HullBlockCount
properties.doc: Hull blocks over the whole sphere BEFORE the band and shaft are cut. Density is the entire trick. At 1,000 you get a low-poly ball; at 6,000 the panel seams and depth variation start reading as plating, which is what makes the reference image look like a machine rather than a shape.

properties.name: GreebleClusterCount
properties.doc: Clusters, not instances. Each drops several boxes of related size.

properties.name: WindowFraction
properties.doc: Fraction of eligible hull blocks that get a lit window.

properties.name: AntennaCount
properties.doc: Antenna spars, each with a beacon at the tip.

properties.name: BillboardCount
properties.doc: Large dark plates for signage. Flat panels with their own material slot, so a decal or a lettered texture can go on them later. Procedural lettering was not worth the machinery; the reference's giant hull text is a texture on a flat face and this is that face.

properties.name: bBuildDeck
properties.doc: Build the landing deck that fills the lower half of the band.

properties.name: DeckThickness
properties.doc: Deck thickness, cm.

properties.name: LandingPadCount
properties.doc: Lit circles marking set-down points.

properties.name: bBuildControlTower
properties.doc: A stack of greebled blocks at the deck edge, lit, to give the deck a horizon.

properties.name: DeckClutterCount
properties.doc: Container stacks and gantries scattered across the deck.

properties.name: bBuildHoloSimEntrance
properties.doc: Build the Holo-sim entrance building on the deck. A substantial structure - a 240 m block, not a doorframe - because a human-scale door on a 1.1 km deck is invisible. The door itself is human-scale, set into a lit recess with an approach lane marked out to it.

properties.name: bBuildContainmentField
properties.doc: Translucent curtain across the band openings. The thing that explains why the deck has air in it while being open to space. Off unless a material is assigned, because an unassigned translucent cylinder renders as an opaque grey wall across every entrance, which is precisely the cage that was asked not to happen.

properties.name: Seed
properties.doc: Seeded so the same station rebuilds identically. Separate from the system seed.

properties.name: BlockSizeFraction
properties.doc: Size unit for STRUCTURES - pylons, arms, gantries, deck furniture - as a fraction of hull radius. Deliberately not used for hull blocks. Those are sized from the block COUNT so they tile: on an evenly spread sphere each block owns 4*pi*R^2/Count of surface, and anything smaller than that leaves a gap. Driving them from a fraction of the radius instead covered about 43% of the sphere at the default count - a hull you could see straight through.

properties.name: DepthJitter
properties.doc: How far block depth may vary, as a fraction of block size. Drives the plated look.

properties.name: Kit
properties.doc: The modelled pieces. Materials live on the assets, not here.

properties.name: ContainmentMaterial
properties.doc: Translucent. Leave empty and the containment curtain is skipped entirely.

properties.name: Buckets
properties.doc: One ISM per kit piece, created on demand. A map rather than named members because the kit is data: adding a piece should not mean adding a component, a clear, a material assign and a switch case in four places. Components are made at Rebuild time, which is legal outside a constructor as long as they are registered - see BucketFor.

properties.name: HoloSimDoorLocal
properties.doc: Filled during the build so GetHoloSimDoorWorld has something to answer with. UPROPERTY FOR THE SAME REASON `Buckets` IS ONE, AND THIS IS NOT COSMETIC. Rebuild() runs from OnConstruction, which does NOT re-run when the editor world is duplicated for PIE - the duplicated actor's UPROPERTYs come across and everything else resets to its initialiser. Left as plain members, these three arrived in PIE as (0,0,0)/false while `Buckets` arrived full, so BeginPlay's `if (Buckets.Num() == 0) Rebuild();` guard skipped the rebuild that would have set them, GetHoloSimDoorWorld answered false, and AHoloSimDoor::EnsureAtStation silently declined to spawn a door. The result was a station with a hall, an approach lane and no interaction anywhere - with nothing in the log, because "no hall means no door" is a legitimate answer that early-out cannot distinguish from this.

classes.name: UCosmicStatsComponent
classes.doc: Health / Mana / Stamina for anything that can fight or die - the player and every enemy share this one component, so damage, death and regen behave identically on both sides. Each pool regenerates, but only after a quiet period since it was last spent or damaged. That delay is what gives stamina its teeth in a zero-lock combat model: since animations never root the character, the only thing stopping endless action-mashing is running the bar dry and waiting for it to come back.

functions.name: SetPendingKiller
functions.sig: void SetPendingKiller(const FString& Name) { KillerName = Name; }
functions.doc: Set the cause of death for hazards that bypass ApplyDamage entirely - falling into a star, the black hole, drowning in the core. Call before whatever kills the pawn so the death screen can name it.

functions.name: ApplyDamage
functions.sig: float ApplyDamage(float Amount, AActor* DamageInstigator = nullptr);
functions.doc: --- Mutation --- Returns the damage actually applied (0 if invulnerable or already dead).

functions.name: AddPeriodicEffect
functions.sig: void AddPeriodicEffect(float PerSecond, float Duration, bool bDamage, AActor* EffectInstigator = nullptr);
functions.doc: Apply a repeating heal (bDamage = false) or damage (bDamage = true) of PerSecond magnitude for Duration seconds. Damage routes through ApplyDamage so death and killer attribution still fire; heals route through Heal. This is what backs the spell system's regeneration, poison and burn effects. A fresh call with the same instigator+sign refreshes rather than stacks, so re-poisoning a target tops up its duration instead of piling on timers.

functions.name: HasDamageOverTime
functions.doc: True while any damage-over-time effect is ticking (drives HUD tinting).

functions.name: TrySpend
functions.doc: Spend if affordable. Returns false and spends NOTHING when either pool is short, so an action never half-pays for itself.

functions.name: CanAfford
functions.sig: bool CanAfford(float ManaAmount, float StaminaAmount) const;

functions.name: ResetAll
functions.doc: Refill everything and clear death (respawn).

functions.name: TrySpendGold
functions.doc: Deducts and returns true only if the full amount was available - never leaves a partial purchase or a negative balance.

functions.name: TickPeriodicEffects
functions.doc: Advance and apply all periodic effects. Split out of TickComponent so the order (effects before regen) is explicit.

properties.name: MaxHealth
properties.doc: --- Health ---

properties.name: HealthRegenPerSecond
properties.doc: Health regenerated per second, once HealthRegenDelay has passed since the last damage taken. 0 disables health regen entirely.

properties.name: MaxMana
properties.doc: --- Mana: the cost of the big abilities ---

properties.name: MaxStamina
properties.doc: --- Stamina: the throttle on zero-lock action spam ---

properties.name: StaminaRegenPerSecond
properties.doc: Deliberately brisk: stamina should feel like a rhythm, not a wall. It stops you holding every key at once without making you stand around.

properties.name: bInvulnerable
properties.doc: While true, damage is ignored entirely (post-death grace, cutscenes).

properties.name: GoldBounty
properties.doc: Paid to whoever lands the killing blow on this actor.

classes.name: ACosmicSun
classes.doc: An editable star: colour, brightness, size, transparency, and solar flares. The previous demos built their sun out of loose parts - a StaticMeshActor for the ball, a PointLight next to it, a second mesh for the halo - all configured by the setup script and unrelated to each other afterwards. Nothing tied them together, so changing the sun's colour meant editing three actors and hoping they matched, and there was no way at all to make it flicker. This is one actor that owns all of it. Every property applies LIVE (in the editor via PostEditChangeProperty, at runtime via ApplySunSettings), and t…

functions.name: ApplySunSettings
functions.doc: Push every current property into the components. Safe to call any time - the options menu and the editor both go through this, so there is exactly one place where settings become appearance.

functions.name: CurrentBrightnessScale
functions.doc: Combined shimmer + flare multiplier for this instant, centred on 1.

properties.name: Core
properties.doc: The visible ball.

properties.name: Corona
properties.doc: A larger, fainter shell around the core. Two nested translucent spheres read as a glowing atmosphere far more convincingly than one ever does, because the overlap gives a natural falloff toward the rim.

properties.name: Light
properties.doc: Local illumination for anything near the star.

properties.name: KeyLight
properties.doc: The scene's key light. A point light at the centre of a 100 km arena cannot reach the outer planets at any sane intensity - inverse-square falloff makes "bright enough out there" mean "blinding up close". So the star carries a directional light too: the point light sells being NEAR it, the directional one actually lights the field.

properties.name: SunColor
properties.doc: Colour of the star, its glow and its light. One value drives all three - they were three separate settings before, which is how they drifted apart.

properties.name: SunRadius
properties.doc: Radius of the core in cm.

properties.name: CoronaScale
properties.doc: Corona size as a multiple of the core. 1 = no visible glow.

properties.name: CoreOpacity
properties.doc: Opacity of the core, 0 = invisible, 1 = solid. Below 1 the star reads as gas you can see into rather than a painted ball.

properties.name: CoronaOpacity
properties.doc: Opacity of the corona shell. Deliberately much lower than the core - the glow should suggest volume, not wrap the star in a second skin.

properties.name: Glow
properties.doc: Emissive brightness of the ball itself (how blown-out it looks).

properties.name: KeyIntensity
properties.doc: Directional key-light brightness (lux). This is what lights the arena.

properties.name: PointIntensity
properties.doc: Point-light brightness (CANDELAS), for being close to the star. Defaults matched to what ACelestialBody does for a Star, because that is what demo2's sun actually was and this looked nothing like it: 4e8 candelas with a 1.2e7 reach and a source radius equal to the ball. My first pass used 5e6, roughly eighty times dimmer - the star lit almost nothing, so there was no bloom off it and it read as a flat painted sphere rather than a light source. Intensity units are set explicitly for the same reason: the default unit is not candelas, so a raw number here would have meant something else entirely.

properties.name: PointRadius
properties.doc: How far the point light reaches (cm).

properties.name: CoreMaterial
properties.doc: Material for the ball. Assign an EMISSIVE or clear-glass material - the engine's default BasicShapeMaterial has no emissive input worth driving, so left on that the sun is a lit grey sphere no matter how the glow is set.

properties.name: CoronaMaterial
properties.doc: Material for the corona shell. Demo2 used clear automotive glass here.

properties.name: bFlaresEnabled

properties.name: TetrominoShape
properties.doc: TETROMINO planets. When this is anything but None it OVERRIDES PoolShape: the planet is built from four cube cells instead of a die, rendered as four instances and collided as four boxes on a single compound body. It has to be a separate property rather than another EDieShape entry because the two go down completely different paths - a die is one convex hull and one static mesh, a tetromino is four of each. Five of the seven pieces are concave, and a single hull of a concave piece is its filled outline: the notch would become invisible floor and pieces could never interlock. See Tetromino.h.

properties.doc: Cube instances making up a tetromino planet. Empty (and hidden) for every other shape. Instanced rather than four components because the arena runs a hundred of these and they all share one mesh and material.

properties.name: PoolSleepSpeed
properties.doc: tuned for 0.1-10 m dice, applied to a 3 km planet. It is far too coarse here, and it broke the arena's centre pull outright: CenterPull is 40 cm/s^2, so from rest it needs 1.25 s to reach 50 cm/s. box3d parks a body after ~0.5 s below threshold. The pull could never outrun the sleep, so every frame it woke a ball, nudged it, and watched box3d zero the velocity again - the sawtooth in the 2026-08-20 probe logs, where velocity ramps 0 -> 20 cm/s and resets, forever, in exactly the pull direction (dot product 1.0000). 5 cm/s is a quarter of what the pull reaches inside one sleep window, so the pull now wins, while a planet drifting slower than 1.8 m per minute still counts as parked and stops costing solver time.

properties.name: PoolRestitution
properties.doc: box3d material for planet-planet contact.

properties.name: MaxPoolSpeed
properties.doc: Hard cap on this planet's linear speed (cm/s). Normal drift is ~1e4 (100 m/s); this is ~30x that, high enough that a bomb still visibly launches a planet but low enough that repeated shoves can't accumulate into the box3d float32 solver blow-up that tripped the renderer NaN breakpoint. Applied every tick.

properties.name: MaxPoolSpin
properties.doc: revolution every 3.6 SECONDS. The 09-06 log caught the frame doing its job perfectly at that rate - `up`, `probe` and `charUp` tracking together with `upVsProbe` pinned at 13 degrees while `up` swung 35 degrees in six frames - and a correct camera faithfully following a world that turns over every 3.6 s is still a tumble dryer. Nothing downstream can fix that; it is the number. 0.25 rad/s is 14 deg/s, a revolution every 25 s. A bomb visibly sets a planet turning and you can stand on it while it does. Headroom is enormous: even a one-second hitch is 14 degrees, nowhere near the half-turn wrap. THIS IS THE DIAL. If bombs should feel wilder or calmer, change it here rather than damping the camera - damping the camera is what produced every bug in the 08-31..09-02 sequence.

properties.name: PoolPlanetAngularDamping
properties.doc: Angular damping for THIS planet's box3d body, applied at creation. Planets already had angular damping - UBox3DWorldSubsystem stamps its shared PoolAngularDamping (0.35, roughly a 2 s half-life) into every body def, which is why a knocked planet visibly settles. But that value is SHARED WITH THE DICE FIELD and is also what the options-menu slider drives, so there was no way to tune planet spin decay without moving the dice too. This is the planet's own knob, defaulted to the same 0.35 so behaviour is unchanged until someone deliberately changes it. Deliberately NOT the fix for bomb spin. Damping governs how fast a planet settles AFTER you stop hitting it; while you are still bombing, the spin simply sits at MaxPoolSpin above. That cap is the dial for how violent bombing feels; this one is for how long the aftermath lasts.

properties.name: PoolSpinGain
properties.doc: Arcade gain on the spin an off-centre weapon/bomb hit imparts. A physically exact off-centre impulse barely rotates a planet-mass body, so this scales it up to something visible. 0 = weapons impart no spin (pure linear knock).
