functions.doc: Place (or move) one of Owner's two portals: destroys whichever portal of that colour they already owned, stands the replacement up in front of them, and re-links the pair. Null if there is nowhere to put it.

functions.name: ClearFor
functions.doc: Remove both of a character's portals.

functions.name: GetOwnerLabel
functions.sig: const FString& GetOwnerLabel() const { return OwnerLabel; }

functions.name: BuildFrame
functions.doc: Lay the frame bars out for the current style's shape. Bars are created on demand and reused, so switching between a 4-bar rectangle and a 24-segment ring does not leak components.

functions.name: ShowCloneOf
functions.doc: Point the clone at a character's mesh and place it mirrored, or hide it.

functions.name: RelinkOwner
functions.sig: static void RelinkOwner(UWorld* World, APawn* Owner);

properties.name: PortalHeight
properties.doc: Opening size (cm), copied from the owner's equipped style at placement. Height matches a character so walking in reads right.

properties.name: Style
properties.doc: The look this portal was built with. Snapshotted rather than looked up live, so changing your equipped style does not restyle portals you have already placed - they are objects in the world, not a live view of a setting.

properties.name: MaxCaptureDistance
properties.doc: Stop capturing past this distance from the viewer (cm).

properties.name: Surface
properties.doc: The see-through quad. Fixed to the actor; two-sided material so the opening is visible from behind as well.

properties.name: Frame
properties.doc: Four slim bars around the opening, wearing a normal LIT translucent glass material with a coloured fresnel glow on top. Reflective on purpose - reflections on the FRAME were never what was reported as a problem. The actual complaint was a separate glass PANE that used to sit directly in front of the portal opening, competing with the see-through render for the same patch of screen; that pane is gone. The frame stands beside the view, not on top of it, so its reflections have nothing to compete with. (An earlier pass forced this material unlit to kill reflections everywhere, including here, which was a misreading of the original complaint - reverted.) The fresnel-driven emissive glow (brightest at grazing angles) is layered on top of the ordinary lit glass for the frame's colour and shape.

properties.name: Effect
properties.doc: Optional per-style flourish at the rim. Most styles leave this empty: particles across the opening fight the view, which is the point of the thing.

properties.name: Clone
properties.doc: A copy of whoever is currently standing in the PARTNER portal, drawn at the mirrored transform so you watch yourself emerge from this side. The half of the clone that has not "come through" yet is behind this portal's opaque surface from the viewer's position, so the depth buffer cuts it off for free - no clip plane, and no edits to the character's materials. See ShowCloneOf().

classes.name: FPortalStyle
classes.doc: What one portal looks like, and the wardrobe of styles a character owns. A style is pure appearance: shape of the opening, the frame that rings it, the colour, and an optional Niagara flourish. Deliberately nothing that affects gameplay - no cooldowns, no ranges, no larger crossing box that would make an expensive portal easier to run through than a cheap one. Collecting these is a wardrobe, not a power curve, so a new style can be added without anyone having to rebalance anything. SHAPES ARE GENERATED, NOT MODELLED. The frame is assembled at runtime from small bars laid out along an arch, el…

properties.name: Id
properties.doc: Stable key. Used for ownership and for the equipped selection, so it must not change once a style has shipped.

properties.name: Price
properties.doc: Cost in gold. Zero means it is owned from the start.

properties.name: FrameThickness
properties.doc: Bar thickness (cm) and how many segments a curved shape is built from. More segments is smoother and more draw calls.

properties.name: Width
properties.doc: Opening size (cm). Kept per-style so an oval can be a different aspect to an arch, but every style is close to character height on purpose - see the note at the top about not selling advantages.

properties.name: FrameMaterial
properties.doc: Overrides the default unlit fresnel rim. Soft, so a missing asset costs the look and not the portal.

properties.name: Effect
properties.doc: Optional flourish, spawned at the rim. Off by default: the see-through view is the point of a portal and particles across it fight the view.

properties.name: ColorScale
properties.doc: Multiplies the pair colour (blue or red). Lets a style read as "icy blue / ember red" while the pair still tells you which end is which - which is the one thing a cosmetic must never obscure.

classes.name: APortalVendor
classes.doc: A kiosk you walk up to in order to BUY portal styles. Deliberately dumb, exactly like AAppearanceMannequin: it knows it is a shop and nothing else. Proximity, the interact key and the window all belong to the HUD, because that is where every other binding and prompt in this project already lives, and because "which interactable is the player nearest" has to be decided once per frame rather than argued over by every interactable. WHY A KIOSK AT ALL, when the wardrobe window opens from a key anywhere: buying is the part that should cost you a trip. Re-equipping something you already own is free…

functions.name: GetLabel
functions.sig: const FString& GetLabel() const { return DisplayLabel; }

properties.name: InteractRadius
properties.doc: How close the player has to be to trade (cm).

properties.name: Sign
properties.doc: A slowly turning marker so the kiosk is findable from a distance.

classes.name: UPortalWardrobeComponent
classes.doc: What portal styles a character owns and which one they are wearing. Self-installing, like UCosmicAppearanceComponent: the player pawn is a Blueprint, and a setup step that has to be done by hand in the editor is a setup step that gets forgotten and then reported as a bug. The vendor and the shop window both call Get(Pawn), which creates it on first use. SESSION-ONLY. Nothing here is serialised yet, so gold and purchases reset on restart. That was a deliberate choice to get the mechanics working first; when a SaveGame arrives it needs exactly two things from here - the owned set and the equipp…

functions.name: Get
functions.doc: Find the pawn's wardrobe, creating one if this is the first time anything has asked. Never returns null for a valid pawn.

functions.name: GetCatalog
functions.sig: const TArray<FPortalStyle>& GetCatalog() const { return Catalog; }

functions.name: GetEquipped
functions.doc: The style new portals are built from. Always valid - falls back to the first catalog entry, which is free and therefore always owned.

functions.name: Purchase
functions.doc: Buy it. Fails (and changes nothing) if the id is unknown, already owned, or the owner cannot afford it.

functions.name: Equip
functions.doc: Wear something already owned. Re-equipping is free and always allowed, which is why it is separate from Purchase.

properties.name: ExtraStyles
properties.doc: Styles appended from data. The built-ins are added first so a project with no data assets still has a full shop.

classes.name: UShieldQuadrantComponent
classes.doc: Quadrant shields: Forward / Right / Rear / Left. An impact drains the quadrant facing it; shields regenerate after a quiet period. If an impact lands on a depleted quadrant, the ship (character) is lost -> respawn via UCosmicFlightComponent. A PURE DAMAGE SINK, AND DELIBERATELY SO SINCE 2026-08-27. This component used to reach OUT for its own damage: it bound OnActorHit, cast the other actor to AAsteroid, and ran a 0.15 s all-actors scan looking for rocks and ring annuli to be hit by. That inverted the dependency - a shield system that knows what an asteroid is - and when asteroids and rings…

functions.name: GetShield
functions.sig: float GetShield(EShieldQuadrant Quadrant) const { return Shields[(int32)Quadrant]; }

functions.name: GetShieldFraction
functions.sig: float GetShieldFraction(EShieldQuadrant Quadrant) const { return Shields[(int32)Quadrant] / MaxShield; }

functions.name: RegisterImpact
functions.sig: void RegisterImpact(const FVector& ImpactPoint, float Damage);
functions.doc: Apply damage from a world-space impact point.

functions.name: AbsorbCrashDamage
functions.sig: float AbsorbCrashDamage(const FVector& ImpactPoint, float Damage);
functions.doc: Soak a CRASH into the quadrant facing the impact and return whatever is left over to be paid by the hull. Unlike RegisterImpact this never destroys the ship itself - the flight component owns that decision - so a crash on a dead quadrant simply passes straight through to the hull. This is what makes "bounce and crash along a surface when shields have failed" work: while a quadrant still holds, scraping it costs shield only.

functions.name: QuadrantFor
functions.doc: Index of the quadrant facing a world-space point, or -1 if unavailable.

properties.name: RegenDelay
properties.doc: Seconds without damage before regen starts.

classes.name: FCosmicShapeWeight
classes.doc: One shape option in the procedural bag, with a relative weight. Mirrors demo4's TETROMINOES list: [("I", 2), ("O", 3), ...]. A tetromino entry sets TetrominoShape and ignores DieShape; anything else uses DieShape. That is the same either/or rule APoolPlanet already enforces, expressed as data instead of as a branch in the script.

properties.name: DieShape
properties.doc: Used when TetrominoShape is None.

properties.name: TetrominoShape
properties.doc: Anything other than None makes this a tetromino and overrides DieShape.

properties.name: Weight
properties.doc: Relative likelihood. 0 disables without deleting the row.

classes.name: FCosmicDieMesh
classes.doc: Render mesh for one die shape. Tetromino planets build themselves from BlockMesh cubes, but a die-shaped planet needs an actual polyhedron on its Mesh component. Without one it spawns invisible - which reads as "every planet is a tetromino", because the tetrominoes are the only ones you can see. An array rather than a TMap keyed by enum: TMap round-trips through FJsonObjectConverter unreliably, and this schema has already lost data that way twice.

classes.name: FCosmicFixedBody
classes.doc: A body placed explicitly, bypassing the procedural pass. For the star, a black hole, a landmark - anything whose position is part of the design rather than an outcome of the seed.

properties.name: Location
properties.doc: World location in cm, relative to the system origin.

properties.name: Radius
properties.doc: Body radius in cm. demo4's sun is 6.0e5 * SCALE.

properties.name: OrbitalGM
properties.doc: mu = G*M, cm^3/s^2. 0 means this body attracts nothing.

properties.name: SurfaceGravity
properties.doc: Walking gravity at the surface, cm/s^2. 980 is Earth.

properties.name: bPinned
properties.doc: Pinned bodies do not move. The star and the black hole normally are.

properties.name: AtmosphereName
properties.doc: Gameplay label for the tint above ("Red", "Blue", ...). See FCosmicPlanetField::AtmosphereTints for why this is a name and not a colour comparison. Optional on a fixed body.

properties.name: Mesh
properties.doc: 1. Its SIMPLE collision is a perfect analytic ball at the circumscribed radius, so anything tracing simple (the spring arm's boom, the build component) resolves metres ABOVE the triangles the ground probe resolves against. The camera boom then starts inside geometry and collapses into the character; build pieces land at chest height. 2. The engine asset is shared with the arena boundary and the nebula, so its collision flags cannot be rewritten without changing those too. SM_PlanetSphere is a 96x48 UV sphere at the SAME 50 cm base radius (ACelestialBody::BaseMeshRadius - do not change that) with CTF_UseComplexAsSimple set, so every query hits the same triangles and the facet dip falls under the skin tolerance. setup_cosmic_demo5.py builds it if it is missing.

classes.name: FCosmicAtmosphereTint
classes.doc: The procedural planet field: demo4's PLANETS / PLANET_R / DIST_IN / DIST_OUT / BREAK_V / ATMO_CHANCE, lifted out of the script. One named entry in an atmosphere palette. The name is gameplay-facing ("Red" is what an enemy patrol filters on); the colour is what renders. Keeping them in one struct is what stops the two drifting - a parallel names array would let a reorder silently relabel every planet in the system.

classes.name: FCosmicPlanetField
classes.doc: A solar system described as DATA rather than as a script that builds one. WHY THIS EXISTS setup_cosmic_demo*.py builds a system by spawning actors from the editor. A dedicated server runs a cooked binary with no editor and no `unreal` Python module, so it cannot run those scripts - it has no way to build a world at all. This type is what a server (or a client, or the editor) reads instead. SEED + RULES, NOT A LIST OF OBJECTS demo4 places 100 planets by seeded random inside distance bands rather than listing each one, and that is kept here deliberately. A definition is a few hundred bytes inst…

properties.name: Count
properties.doc: demo4 uses 100.

properties.name: MinRadius
properties.doc: Radius range in cm, inclusive. demo4: 1.5e5*SCALE .. 2.0e6*SCALE.

properties.name: InnerFraction
properties.doc: Placement band as a fraction of ArenaRadius. demo4 uses 0.14 .. 0.90 - the inner bound is up from demo3's 0.10 specifically to keep the field clear of the now-central sun.

properties.name: BreakVelocity
properties.doc: Initial drift speed in cm/s. NOT scaled with the arena. demo4 calls this out explicitly: it is a speed, not a size, so halving the arena while holding the speed makes the field livelier on purpose. Anyone rescaling a system should leave this alone unless they actually want calmer play.

properties.name: ShapeWeights
properties.doc: Weighted shape bag. Empty means all spheres.

properties.name: PlanetMaterial
properties.doc: Single material for every planet. Ignored when PlanetMaterials is non-empty.

properties.name: PlanetMaterials
properties.doc: Pool of materials, one picked at random per planet. demo4 drew from the Automotive set, which is why its field read as a bowl of mixed metals and glass rather than a hundred identical objects. A single PlanetMaterial makes the arena look like untextured placeholder geometry even when the material itself is fine.

properties.name: AtmosphereTints
properties.doc: silently, because a patrol that spawns nowhere looks exactly like a patrol that has not been written yet. The name is carried onto ACelestialBody::AtmosphereName, so the tint and the label can never disagree: they are assigned from the same entry. Empty falls back to the ACelestialBody default (Earth blue, unnamed). REPLACED the old bare `AtmosphereColors` array on 2026-08-27. A holo-sim spec saved before that date has no AtmosphereTints key and will fall back to the default blue rather than erroring - acceptable while holo-sims are still unproven (M5/M6), and the reason this is a rename rather than a second parallel array nobody would keep in sync.

properties.name: AtmosphereMaterial
properties.doc: Material for the visible atmosphere shell. REQUIRED for an atmosphere to be visible at all. bHasAtmosphere only drives UAtmosphereComponent's scattering; the shell you actually SEE is ShellMesh, and ACelestialBody::ConfigureVisuals only unhides ShellMesh when ShellMaterial is set. demo3 and demo4 both set bHasAtmosphere without ever setting a shell material, so no atmosphere was visible in any run.

properties.name: AtmosphereShellScale
properties.doc: Shell radius as a multiple of the planet radius. demo4 uses 1.12.

properties.name: bScaleAtmosphereChanceWithRadius
properties.doc: Bias atmosphere chance toward bigger planets. demo4: chance * (0.5 + 0.5 * (r - MinRadius) / span), so the smallest planet gets half the base chance and the largest gets the full amount. A pea-sized rock with a glowing halo reads as a bug.

properties.name: EnemyPatrolAtmosphere
properties.doc: Planets whose atmosphere carries this name get an enemy patrol. NAME_None disables patrols entirely. Matched against ACelestialBody::AtmosphereName, which the builder set from the same tint entry that set the colour - so this is a label lookup, not a colour comparison, and it cannot be broken by nudging a channel. Enemy fighters and their spawner have existed and worked for a long time. NOTHING HAD EVER PLACED ONE: Cosmos.umap contained no enemy or fighter string of any kind, which is the whole reason no enemy has ever been seen in this game. Placing them from the builder rather than by hand means the next regenerated system gets them too.

properties.name: EnemyPatrolRadiusMultiplier
properties.doc: Patrol radius as a multiple of the planet's radius. The spawner's own default is a flat 10 km, which is meaningless here: planets in this field range from ~28,000 to ~375,000 cm in radius, so one absolute number would put fighters inside the big ones and a long way from the small ones.

properties.name: DieMeshes
properties.doc: Per-die-shape render meshes. A shape with no entry falls back to FallbackDieMesh.

properties.name: FallbackDieMesh
properties.doc: Used when a die shape has no mesh listed. Defaults to the engine sphere.

properties.name: SunKeepOutMultiplier
properties.doc: Planets are rejected within this multiple of a star's radius. demo4 uses 3.0 and explains why: a planet materialising inside the star is "an instant physics fight" - PoolArenaManager's SunClearance shoves it out every frame and it visibly vibrates in place.

properties.name: PadWellClearanceMultiplier
properties.doc: Pad keep-out is widened by this multiple of the LARGEST planet radius. Not cosmetic. demo4's comment is explicit: the on-foot controller treats roughly 3x a planet's radius as "inside its gravity well", so a planet whose well merely reaches the pad becomes the body the controller thinks owns you while you are standing on the platform. Keeping only the geometry clear is not enough; the wells have to be clear too.

classes.name: FCosmicArena
classes.doc: A solar system described as DATA rather than as a script that builds one. WHY THIS EXISTS setup_cosmic_demo*.py builds a system by spawning actors from the editor. A dedicated server runs a cooked binary with no editor and no `unreal` Python module, so it cannot run those scripts - it has no way to build a world at all. This type is what a server (or a client, or the editor) reads instead. SEED + RULES, NOT A LIST OF OBJECTS demo4 places 100 planets by seeded random inside distance bands rather than listing each one, and that is kept here deliberately. A definition is a few hundred bytes inst…

properties.name: bSpawnArenaManager
properties.doc: Spawn an APoolArenaManager for wall reflection, pockets and scoring.

properties.name: Radius
properties.doc: Boundary sphere radius in cm. demo4: 2.5e7 * SCALE = 4,687,500. This maps to APoolArenaManager::ArenaRadius. demo4 tried to set a property called `boundary_radius`, which does not exist - the real name is `arena_radius`. set_editor_property raises on an unknown name and the surrounding try/except swallowed it, so the wall silently kept its 5,000,000 default. Going through the schema removes the chance to misname it.

properties.name: CenterPull
properties.doc: Gentle pull toward centre, cm/s^2, so loose balls drift back into play.

properties.name: SunClearance
properties.doc: Margin kept between a planet's surface and the star's shell, cm.

classes.name: FCosmicStarField
classes.doc: Instanced-geometry star backdrop. demo2 spawned one of these; demo4 lists "StarField" in its teardown labels but never rebuilds it, so running demo4 after demo2 deletes the backdrop permanently. Making it part of the system definition means a scene cannot lose it by being rebuilt.

properties.name: ShellRadius
properties.doc: Shell distance in cm. NOT multiplied by Spec.Scale. The backdrop is meant to read as effectively infinite; scaling it with the arena would make the stars visibly close in a small system and defeat the point.

properties.name: StarSizeRange
properties.doc: World-space star diameters at the shell, cm.

properties.name: Seed
properties.doc: Separate from the system seed so the sky can stay put while the field rerolls.

properties.name: StarMesh
properties.doc: Defaulted, not left empty. AStarField::OnConstruction early-returns on a null StarMesh and builds nothing - no stars, no warning. An FSoftObjectPath that fails to survive a JSON round-trip would therefore produce a silently empty sky, which is exactly what happened. A default means the worst case is plain white spheres rather than nothing at all.

properties.name: StarMaterial
properties.doc: demo2 uses M_Star: unlit, emissive (20, 20, 26). Left empty by default on purpose - it lives in project content, and Cosmos should not hard-code a path into one specific game. Without it the stars render in the mesh's default material: visible, but lit grey rather than glowing.

classes.name: FCosmicSpawn
classes.doc: Where players enter the system. THE 30 m STARTER PLATFORM IS GONE (2026-08-23). Players arrive on the station; bBuildPlatform, PlatformScale, PlatformMaterial and PlatformTags went with it, along with UCosmosWorldBuilder::SpawnSpawnPlatform and the on-foot controller's bGroundIsPad. Old JSON specs carrying those keys still load - FJsonObjectConverter ignores fields it does not recognise - they simply do nothing now.

properties.name: Offset
properties.doc: Offset from the system origin, cm. Kept along +Z above a central star. The reason outlived the platform: with the star at the origin and the arrival point offset along +Z, the measured normal underfoot and the star's radial agree. In a sun-overhead layout they point opposite ways and players arrive inverted.

properties.name: bSpawnPlayerStart
properties.doc: Spawn an APlayerStart at the arrival point.

properties.name: PlayerStartHeight
properties.doc: Height of the PlayerStart above the surface it stands on, cm.

properties.name: KeepOutRadius
properties.doc: Keep-out radius around the spawn, cm. 0 falls back to DefaultKeepOut. ONLY CONSULTED WHEN THERE IS NO STATION. A station derives its clearance from its own geometry (StationKeepOut) - much larger, and impossible to disagree with the thing it is protecting. This is the bare arrival point's radius, and since the platform that used to imply it is gone there is nothing left to derive it from.

classes.name: FCosmicStationSpec
classes.doc: that a builder turns into actors. THE ONLY ARRIVAL STRUCTURE, as of 2026-08-23. It used to merely supersede FCosmicSpawn::bBuildPlatform; that platform is gone, so bEnabled now chooses between a station and a bare PlayerStart in open space. The original note is kept because it is why the platform went rather than staying as a fallback - having both would leave a 30 m slab floating inside a 1.2 km hangar. The dimensions here are absolute cm and are deliberately NOT multiplied by FSolarSystemSpec::Scale. The arena and the planet field scale together because they are a layout; a station is a bui…

properties.name: HullRadius
properties.doc: Hull radius, cm. 60,000 is a 1.2 km sphere.

properties.name: SlotHalfHeight
properties.doc: Half-height of the equatorial band. 15,000 gives a 300 m mouth.

properties.name: PolarShaftRadius
properties.doc: Radius of the shaft through the north pole. 0 closes it.

properties.name: HullBlockCount
properties.doc: Density is the whole trick. Below ~2,000 it stops reading as plating.

properties.name: bSpawnHoloSimDoor
properties.doc: Spawn a sliding pocket door in the Holo-sim entrance recess.

properties.name: Seed
properties.doc: Seeded separately from the system, so the station stays put when the field rerolls.

properties.name: WindowMaterial
properties.doc: Emissive. Without it the windows are grey boxes and the station looks dead.

properties.name: BeaconMaterial
properties.doc: Emissive red.

properties.name: ContainmentMaterial
properties.doc: Translucent. Left empty the containment curtain is skipped, not drawn opaque.

properties.name: Tags
properties.doc: Actor tags for the station. "StableGround" is load-bearing for the same reason it is on the platform: it is what gives the deck a fixed "up" instead of the on-foot frame falling through to a planet's radial.

classes.name: FSolarSystemSpec
classes.doc: A complete system. This is the runtime currency - both the DataAsset and the hub's JSON resolve to one of these before anything is spawned.

functions.name: IsValid
functions.sig: bool IsValid() const { return Arena.Radius > 0.0 && Scale > 0.0; }

properties.name: SystemId
properties.doc: Stable id. For Holo-sim this is the row id in the hub.

properties.name: Seed
properties.doc: Same seed, same system, always. This is what makes seed-based generation safe for multiplayer: the server builds from the seed, and any client that needs to predict can derive the identical layout without being sent 100 transforms.

properties.name: Scale
properties.doc: Uniform scale applied to every LENGTH here, matching demo4's SCALE. Applied by the builder, not baked into the values, so a system can be rescaled without re-deriving every number. Note demo4's warning: the scale must be applied ONCE. Halving the arena and then separately halving planet radii made them a quarter size against a half-size arena, which read as "punier" rather than "same field, smaller".

properties.name: Station
properties.doc: When enabled, replaces Spawn's platform entirely. See FCosmicStationSpec.

properties.name: FixedBodies
properties.doc: Applied after the procedural pass, so these always win.

properties.name: Metadata
properties.doc: Free-form, for game-specific data the schema does not model.

classes.name: FCosmicSpecParseResult
classes.doc: Result of parsing a spec from JSON. A single struct return rather than `bool Fn(Json, FSpec& Out, FString& Err)`. The out-param form is fine in C++ but ambiguous through UE's Python binding - how many values come back in the tuple depends on how UHT classified each reference, and getting it wrong is a runtime unpack error rather than a compile error. One return value has exactly one shape.

classes.name: USolarSystemDefinition
classes.doc: The cooked-asset form. Create these in the editor under Content/CosmicDemo/Systems/.

classes.name: ASpellProjectile
classes.doc: Physics-aware spell bolt: fireball, ice shard, lightning, poison glob, etc. Modelled on ATorpedo (manual swept flight so it never tunnels a planet), but its payload is the spell layer rather than the weapon layer: it deals UCosmicStatsComponent damage, can plant a damage-over-time band on what it hits, can return a slice of that damage to the caster (life-tap), and it shoves any box3d body it strikes so spells interact with the physics world exactly like the ship weapons do. Fired by UCosmicAbilityComponent for any FCosmicAbilityDef whose Shape is Projectile. Everything about it is configured…

functions.name: Configure
functions.sig: void Configure(class ACharacter* InCaster, const FVector& Dir, const struct FCosmicAbilityDef& Def);
functions.doc: One-call setup. Caster is used for damage attribution, life-tap healing and to ignore the body the bolt launched from.

functions.name: GetFlightVelocity
functions.doc: Read/redirect the flight vector. A portal rotates this into the exit's frame so a bolt fired into one comes out of the other still travelling, rather than stopping dead or keeping a heading that now points into a wall. Speed is the caller's business - the portal preserves it.

functions.name: SetFlightVelocity
functions.sig: void SetFlightVelocity(const FVector& NewVelocity) { Velocity = NewVelocity; }

functions.name: HitActor
functions.sig: float HitActor(AActor* Target, const FVector& At, const FVector& Dir);
functions.doc: Resolve one struck actor: stats damage, DoT, life-tap, knockback, popups. Returns the damage actually dealt (for splash bookkeeping).

functions.name: Detonate
functions.sig: void Detonate(const FVector& At, AActor* DirectHit);
functions.doc: Detonate: direct hit (no splash) or an area sweep (splash) at At.

classes.name: AStarField
classes.doc: A starfield made of real geometry: N tiny unlit-emissive spheres instanced on a distant shell. Unlike shader noise, this can't alias into a white-out and costs one draw call.

functions.name: OnConstruction
functions.sig: virtual void OnConstruction(const FTransform& Transform) override;

properties.name: StarSizeRange
properties.doc: World-space star diameters (cm) at the shell distance.

classes.name: UPhxAccountSettings
classes.doc: Phx Account - project settings. Everything configurable lives here so the plugin has no hard-coded URLs and stays sellable. Edit under Project Settings > Plugins > Phx Account, which writes to Config/DefaultGame.ini.

functions.name: GetAdvertisedAddress
functions.sig: void GetAdvertisedAddress(const UObject* WorldContextObject, FString& OutHost, int32& OutPort) const;
functions.doc: Resolves AdvertisedHost/Port against -PhxHost= / -PhxPort= command line overrides.

functions.name: GetResolvedServerName
functions.sig: FString GetResolvedServerName(const FString& Host, int32 Port) const;
functions.doc: ServerName, or "host:port" when unset. Honours -PhxServerName=.

functions.name: GetResolvedRegion
functions.doc: Region, honouring -PhxRegion=.

functions.name: GetNormalizedBaseUrl
functions.doc: BaseUrl with any trailing slash stripped, so callers can just append paths.

properties.name: BaseUrl
properties.doc: Root URL of the account hub, no trailing slash. e.g. https://your-host.com (dev: http://localhost:4000)

properties.name: GameSlug
properties.doc: The `slug` column of the `games` row for this title. Must match exactly; the hub 404s on an unknown slug rather than guessing.

properties.name: RequestTimeoutSeconds
properties.doc: Seconds before an in-flight request is abandoned.

properties.name: ServerApiKeyEnvVar
properties.doc: Server-only. Name of the environment variable holding the shared `GAMES_SERVER_API_KEY` secret. It is read from the environment rather than stored in an ini on purpose: ini files get cooked into client builds, and this key lets its holder act on behalf of ANY user. It must never ship to a client.

properties.name: bRequireVerifiedEmail
properties.doc: Server-only. Reject a joining player whose account has not verified its email. Off by default so playtests aren't blocked by mail delivery.

properties.name: bAdvertiseToHub
properties.doc: Server-only. Register with the hub so clients can discover this shard.

properties.name: bAdvertiseFromPIE
properties.doc: - It publishes a 127.0.0.1 row into whichever hub BaseUrl names. Against a PRODUCTION hub that row is visible to real players and resolves to their own machine. - It claims that host:port, so any admin command queued for that row is delivered to it. A queued `shutdown` reached a PIE session and called FPlatformMisc::RequestExit, which in-process means the EDITOR exits. classes.name: ARSSFrontEndGameState
classes.doc: The client-visible mirror of the front end's menu config. MenuWidgetClass lives here, not on the game mode, because AGameModeBase only exists on the server / listen host. A remote client in a real client-server session never has a game mode instance at all - that is not a bug, it is how the engine works - so GetAuthGameMode() correctly returns null there and cannot be the thing that hands the client its menu class. GameStateBase is the engine's own answer to "data the game mode owns but every client needs to see": it replicates automatically to everyone, including a dedicated server's remote…

classes.name: ARSSFrontEndPlayerController
classes.doc: Cursor on, input to the UI, and a camera that is not the world origin. Also where the main menu itself now lives, and where it has to: this is the one object in the front end guaranteed to exist, locally, fully usable, on every machine that actually has a human at the keyboard - the host's own local player if listen-hosted, and every remote client under a real dedicated server. The game mode is neither of those on a remote client, which is exactly why the old GameMode::ShowMainMenu() drew a black screen there.

functions.name: ShowMainMenu
functions.doc: Build the menu and hand the player to it. Called by the intro director, locally, when the sequence ends or is skipped, and by BeginPlay when there is no director in the map. Idempotent, because those two paths can race on a zero-length sequence. A no-op on any controller that is not locally controlled - that is the server's authoritative copy of a remote client's controller, or a dedicated server with nobody connected yet, and a widget built there would AddToViewport into nothing.

functions.name: TryShowMainMenu
functions.doc: The actual attempt, split from ShowMainMenu() so it can retry itself. MenuWidgetClass is authored on the game mode and reaches this controller by replicating down through ARSSFrontEndGameState. On a remote client that replication can still be in flight the instant the intro finishes - GameState usually arrives early, but "usually" is not a guarantee - so a missing class here is treated as a race and retried for a couple of seconds before it is logged as a real misconfiguration.

classes.name: ARSSFrontEndGameMode

Deliberately its own game mode rather than a mode on the Cosmos map, because everything ARSSGameModeBase does - PreLogin validation, character loading, shard heartbeat - is meaningless here and actively in the way. The front end has no server and no session yet; finding one is the entire point of it.

classes.name: ARSSLoginTerminal
classes.doc: Diegetic login terminal. A Cockpit UI panel the player physically walks up to and uses: real 3D buttons for Sign In / Register / Quit, with a flat form hosted on the panel's UWidgetComponent for the two fields that need a keyboard. KEYBOARD INPUT ON A WORLD-SPACE WIDGET IS NOT AUTOMATIC. See BeginTextEntry() and the README - the pawn needs a UWidgetInteractionComponent, and the player controller needs to be in GameAndUI input mode. Without both, the buttons work and typing does not, which is a confusing way to discover the requirement.

classes.doc: The flat main menu: sign in, pick a character, fly. The DIEGETIC terminal (ARSSLoginTerminal) is the other half of this plugin and they deliberately do not share a base class. That one is a physical panel you walk up to inside a world that is already running; this one runs before any world exists, over a cinematic, with a mouse cursor. Trying to make one class do both would mean a class that is always in the wrong input mode for half its life. WHAT LIVES WHERE. Everything that talks to the hub is in C++, here. The WBP subclass supplies layout and calls the BlueprintCallable entry points below…

functions.name: GetRenderAlpha
functions.sig: float GetRenderAlpha() const { return FixedDt > 0.0f ? FMath::Clamp(Accumulator / FixedDt, 0.0f, 1.0f) : 0.0f; }
functions.doc: Fixed-timestep RENDER INTERPOLATION support. Physics advances in discrete FixedDt steps, so a render frame that triggers zero steps would show a frozen transform and a frame with a step would jump - visible mesh jitter, worst at points far from a body's centre (dice corners). Mirror code should interpolate between a body's previous and current step transforms by this alpha (0..1 = fraction of the way from the previous step to the current).
